101354P2.intro: An hour in the saddle on the old lava trails of Vesuvius, at a walking pace, with a guide who talks you through the eruptions and the civilisations the volcano left its mark on. The horses follow ancient tracks between vineyards growing on volcanic soil, and every bend opens up a view of the bay. This isn’t a ride for anyone who wants to gallop: it’s about spending time with the animals and taking in the scenery. Two hours in total, with helmet, water and a shuttle from Pompei Scavi included.
cosaSiFa: You set off from Pompei Scavi on the shuttle that climbs to the starting point on the slopes of the volcano. There you’re matched with your horse, put on a helmet and get the basic instructions. The pace stays at a walk the whole way: if you’re after speed you’ll be disappointed, if you want to look around you’re in the right place.

The route follows the old lava trails, through vineyards and open stretches with views over the bay and the countryside below. The guide, in English or Spanish, explains how the eruptions shaped the landscape and what happened to the towns at the foot of the volcano. There are stops for photos, and plenty of viewpoints to choose from.

The ride itself lasts about an hour; with the shuttle, getting ready and heading back, it comes to two hours. Groups are capped at 10 people and water is included. You finish where you started, and the shuttle takes you back to Pompei Scavi.
101354P2.perChi: For anyone who wants to see Vesuvius without hiking up to the crater, and for animal lovers: the pace is slow and the focus is on the landscape. Good for families with older kids and for couples. Not for adrenaline seekers or anyone who wants to gallop; the guide speaks English or Spanish, not Italian.
101354P2.consiglio: Long trousers and closed shoes, no sandals: you need them in the saddle and on the lava. Bring a hat and sunscreen, as there’s little shade on the volcano. Pair it with the ruins of Pompeii, since the shuttle leaves from there: ruins in the morning, horses in the afternoon, or the other way round. Book early in the warmer months, as groups are ten people at most.

faq.q: How long does it last and where does it start?
faq.a: About 2 hours in total, around one of them in the saddle. You start from Pompei Scavi with the included shuttle, which drives up the slopes of Vesuvius and brings you back at the end. Groups are capped at 10 people.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: The helmet, water, the shuttle to and from Pompei Scavi, the horse and the guide who leads the group along the lava trails. Nothing else is included: bring what you need for the sun and to be comfortable in the saddle.

faq.q: Do we gallop? What language does the guide speak?
faq.a: No. The ride is at a walk, designed for spending time with the horses and enjoying the view, not for going fast. The guide speaks English and Spanish. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start.

101354P7.intro: Two hours inside the ruins with an expert guide and a group of no more than twenty. The skip-the-line ticket is included, and you meet at the Porta Marina Superiore entrance. You’ll see theatres, temples and bath complexes, with the guide explaining how everyday Roman life worked and pointing out corners you’d walk straight past on your own. If you’re staying in Naples, you can add return transport.
cosaSiFa: Meet ten minutes early at the Porta Marina Superiore entrance, where the guide waits with a green sign. If you’ve chosen the option with transport, a minivan picks you up in Naples in the morning from the designated pickup point. With tickets already in hand, you walk straight in, no ticket office and no queues.

The guided walk lasts two hours and takes you through the city buried in AD 79: the streets, theatres, temples, bath complexes and houses, with the guide describing the daily life of the people who lived there. It’s in English. At the end you leave by the same entrance; if you have transport, the minivan takes you back to Naples.
101354P7.perChi: For anyone getting to Pompeii under their own steam, by train or car, who just wants the guided visit without a full-day package. Suitable for all fitness levels, and pushchairs are allowed. The guide speaks English: if you don’t follow it well, pick a different tour. Private groups can ask for the dedicated option.
101354P7.consiglio: Arrive ten minutes early, as the group leaves on time. Bring water, a hat and closed shoes: the streets are stone and shade is scarce. After booking you’ll get an automatic email with all the instructions, so read it. If you choose transport from Naples, the morning pickup only runs from the designated point.

faq.q: How long is it and where do we meet?
faq.a: The guided visit lasts two hours. You meet outside the Porta Marina Superiore entrance, where the guide holds a green sign, ten minutes before the start time. If you choose the option with transport, you’re picked up in Naples in the morning from the designated pickup point.

faq.q: What language is the tour in?
faq.a: The guide speaks English. Groups are limited to twenty people, so you can follow along and ask questions without shouting. There’s also a private option if you want a visit just for yourselves.

faq.q: What’s included and how do I cancel?
faq.a: The skip-the-line ticket for the ruins and the two-hour guided visit. Transport from Naples is only included in the dedicated option. Tips aren’t included. Pushchairs and wheelchairs are allowed. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before the start.

1032625.intro: A cooking class in a restaurant in the centre, a short walk from the port and the Teatro San Carlo, where you learn fresh pasta from scratch and tiramisù step by step. You start with a glass of prosecco and a Neapolitan starter, cook with the apron and tools provided, and at the end you eat what you’ve made, with a tasting of limoncello or coffee and amaro (a herbal liqueur). The group is small, and the class comes with a certificate and digital recipes. It runs every day except Sunday.
cosaSiFa: You meet at the restaurant. It starts with a welcome glass, prosecco or alcohol-free, and a Neapolitan starter, while the pastry chef who runs the class explains the plan. Then it’s aprons on and on to the pasta: dough kneaded by hand from scratch, rolled out and shaped with traditional Neapolitan tools, every step demonstrated before you do it.

Part two is the tiramisù, from the cream to the assembly, with a tasting of limoncello or meloncello (the melon version), or espresso and amaro. You can ask questions in Italian, English, Spanish or French. Water is unlimited throughout. The group is capped at sixteen people, and everyone actually cooks rather than just watching.

At the end you sit down and eat your own pasta and tiramisù, which make a proper lunch or dinner. You get a diploma and the recipes in digital form, so you can make them again at home. The hands-on part takes about two and a half hours; with the welcome and the meal it comes to three. Free luggage storage is available if you arrive with a suitcase.
1032625.perChi: Ideal for couples, families and solo travellers who want to meet people: you cook side by side and eat together. Also great on your arrival or departure day, thanks to the luggage storage. Not suitable for coeliacs, people with food allergies or diabetics. Babies under one aren’t allowed; older children tend to love the tiramisù part most.
1032625.consiglio: Come hungry, because what you cook is a full meal. Mention any intolerances when you book so they can set up your station. The restaurant is near the port and the Teatro San Carlo: before or after, take in the Galleria Umberto, Palazzo Reale and Piazza del Plebiscito, all a few minutes’ walk away.

faq.q: What language is the class in?
faq.a: Explanations are in Italian and English, and the person running the class also speaks Spanish and French. The group is small, so it’s easy to ask for a step to be repeated. It runs every day except Sunday and lasts about three hours.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: A welcome glass of prosecco or a soft drink, a Neapolitan starter, all the ingredients and tools, an apron to use, water, a tasting of limoncello or meloncello or coffee and amaro, the meal with the dishes you’ve made, the diploma with digital recipes, and luggage storage. Transport and tips aren’t included.

faq.q: Is it suitable for people with intolerances?
faq.a: Not for coeliacs or anyone with serious food allergies: you work with flour, eggs, dairy and coffee in a shared space. The tiramisù isn’t recommended for diabetics. For other needs, it’s best to mention them when booking. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

103374P5.intro: Two and a half hours combining the two things people do most in Naples: eating and looking around. You start from Piazza Bellini and at each stop you taste a different dish, while in between the guide, in English, takes you to the places in the old town worth seeing. Groups of up to 15, tastings included. It’s the tour for anyone with just one afternoon who doesn’t want to choose between the monument and the sandwich.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Bellini, then walk through the old town. The stops are chosen to bring a different flavour to the counter each time: you taste standing up, listen to the explanation and move on. The programme doesn’t list the dishes one by one, but the idea is Neapolitan street food: the specialities people here eat every day.

Between tastings the route passes the main sights of the centre, and the guide talks about them the way a local friend would: what they are, why they matter, what’s round the corner. The pace is relaxed and the distances short, because in the old town everything is close together.
Two and a half hours in all, in English, with a maximum of 15 people. You finish with a full stomach and a clear idea of where to go back to on your own in the following days.
103374P5.perChi: For anyone short on time who wants a single tour covering both the food and the sights of the centre, without going too deep into either. Good for first-timers and groups. Less suited to anyone who doesn’t follow English well or who wants a proper art tour.
103374P5.consiglio: Come hungry and wear comfortable shoes: you eat standing up and walk on basalt paving stones. Piazza Bellini is just behind Via dei Tribunali, so before or after the tour you can stretch your legs to the Duomo or San Gregorio Armeno. Weekend slots fill up, so book ahead.

faq.q: Where does it start and how long is it?
faq.a: You meet in Piazza Bellini, in the old town, and walk for about two and a half hours between food stops and sights. Groups are capped at 15 people.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: The tastings at each stop and the guide. Every stop offers a different speciality, so by the end the tastings add up to a meal. Any extra food or drinks are paid separately.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: The guide speaks English. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund; after that the ticket is non-refundable. It’s worth mentioning any dietary needs when you book.

104566P11.intro: Two and a half hours in the lanes of the old town with an English-speaking guide who knows where Neapolitans stop to eat standing up. You taste fresh buffalo mozzarella, pizza fritta (deep-fried pizza), a slice of margherita, and finish with a small glass of limoncello. Between bites, the guide shares the history and stories of one of the oldest cities in Italy. Groups of up to 15, starting from Piazza Bellini.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Bellini. From there you head into the lanes of the ancient centre and start with buffalo mozzarella, eaten fresh as it should be. Next comes pizza fritta, which people here eat on the move, and a slice of margherita, the oven-baked chapter of the same story.

At every stop the guide explains what you’re eating and tells you about the history of the city and the neighbourhoods you walk through. The last stop is limoncello, a small glass to round things off. It’s two and a half hours of slow walking with frequent stops. The organisers are clear about it: come on an empty stomach.
Groups are capped at 15 people and the tour is in English. The pace is set by the lanes: narrow streets, short stops, lots of people around, especially at weekends and at mealtimes.
104566P11.perChi: For first-timers who want to cover the basics of Neapolitan street food in one afternoon without hunting down the places themselves. Good for groups of friends and solo travellers, since the group is small. Less suited to anyone who doesn’t follow English: the guide only speaks that language.
104566P11.consiglio: Go easy on breakfast and skip lunch: the tastings are a proper meal. Wear comfortable shoes for the paving stones. Piazza Bellini is a stone’s throw from Via dei Tribunali and San Gregorio Armeno, so there’s plenty to walk to before or after. Book ahead for bank holidays and weekends.

faq.q: Where do we meet and how long is it?
faq.a: You start from Piazza Bellini, in the old town, and walk for about two and a half hours through the lanes. It’s on foot at a gentle pace, with frequent stops to eat and listen to the guide.

faq.q: What do we eat and what’s included?
faq.a: The tastings at every stop are included in the ticket: buffalo mozzarella, pizza fritta, a slice of margherita and a small glass of limoncello, plus the guide. Come hungry, as the tastings add up to a meal.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: The guide speaks English. Groups are capped at 15 people. You can cancel for free up to 24 hours before the start for a full refund; after that the ticket is non-refundable.

1098790.intro: A day on a boat between Procida and Ischia, with the skipper choosing the route according to the sea. You leave Molo Beverello by hydrofoil, forty minutes to Procida, and board the boat there. From then on it’s all sea: the Corricella with its coloured houses, the volcanic coast of Ischia, bays to stop and swim in, and a lunch prepared on board, with sparkling wine and soft drinks. You don’t go ashore on Ischia; you see it from the water.
cosaSiFa: Meet at Molo Beverello in Naples. The hydrofoil to Procida is included and takes forty minutes. On arrival you board the boat with the skipper and start by circling the island: Marina Corricella, the fishermen’s houses, the little coves. Then you head for Ischia, sailing along its coast without landing, past volcanic cliffs and hidden inlets.

Along the way there are swim stops in clear water, with the boat anchored in a bay. At some point lunch is served: fresella (a crunchy Neapolitan rusk topped with tomatoes), pasta and fruit prepared on board, with spumante, prosecco or champagne and soft drinks included. In the afternoon you return to Procida, and from there the hydrofoil takes you back to Molo Beverello, another forty minutes. Seven hours in total.
1098790.perChi: For anyone who wants a real day at sea, not a ferry crossing: swims, lunch with wet feet and the islands seen from the water. Works well solo or as a couple, as the group is small. Not for anyone prone to seasickness: the route changes with the waves and the boat moves. Under-18s must be accompanied.
1098790.consiglio: Wear your swimsuit and bring a towel, sunscreen and a camera: there are no towels on board. No heels. If the sea is rough, the skipper changes course to find sheltered bays: that’s not a flaw, it’s the whole point of going on a small boat. Hotel transfers can be requested separately.

faq.q: How long is it and where does it start?
faq.a: Seven hours, from Molo Beverello and back to the same spot. The return hydrofoil to Procida is included, forty minutes each way; you board the boat with the skipper in Procida. Hotel pickup isn’t included but can be arranged separately for a fee.

faq.q: What do we eat and what’s included?
faq.a: An Italian lunch prepared on board with fresella, pasta and fruit; spumante, prosecco or champagne and soft drinks. The swim stops and a professional skipper are included. Bring your own towels and beach gear.

faq.q: Do we land on Ischia? What languages does the skipper speak?
faq.a: No, you sail along Ischia’s coast without going ashore; in Procida you do stop, to switch from the hydrofoil to the boat. The skipper speaks English, Italian and Spanish. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before departure.

113923.intro: Beneath the Rione Sanità lies one of the oldest places of Neapolitan faith: the catacombs linked to San Gennaro, the city’s patron saint. In about three quarters of an hour, a guide in Italian or English leads you through underground basilicas, frescoes over a thousand years old and the mosaics of the Crypt of the Bishops. The ticket also covers the nearby Catacombs of San Gaudioso and the Basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità, to see at your own pace, and supports a regeneration project for the neighbourhood.
cosaSiFa: The entrance is in the Rione Sanità. You go down with the guide into the early Christian cemetery, starting with the oldest part, the upper catacomb, decorated in the 3rd century in the so-called Pompeian style: here are some of the earliest Christian paintings in Italy. Then you move on to the underground basilica dedicated to Sant’Agrippino, around which the site grew in the 4th century.

The guide stops at the baptismal font commissioned by Bishop Paul II, who took refuge here in the 8th century during the iconoclast struggles, and at the Byzantine-style frescoes of the 9th and 10th centuries. The highlight is the Crypt of the Bishops, with 5th-century mosaics, including one portraying San Quodvultdeus, bishop of Carthage.

The visit lasts about 45 minutes and ends with a pass for the Catacombs of San Gaudioso and the Basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità, valid for twelve months: you can see them straight after or on another day. The ticket supports a regeneration project for the Rione Sanità.
113923.perChi: Suitable for everyone, including families and anyone short on time: in under an hour you see one of the oldest things in the city. Lovers of early Christian art and religious history will be in their element; if you’re after spooky caves you may be a little disappointed, as the tone here is historical. The pace is brisk, so bear that in mind if you like to linger.
113923.consiglio: Pair it with the Sanità above ground: the neighbourhood is a few steps away, and the same ticket gets you into San Gaudioso and the Basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità. A morning slot works best, then lunch in the area. It’s cooler underground, so a light jacket helps even in summer. Book the slot in your language.

faq.q: How long is it and what language is it in?
faq.a: The guided visit lasts about 45 minutes and is in Italian or English: you choose the slot when booking, with a fixed start time. The meeting point is the entrance to the catacombs, in the Rione Sanità.

faq.q: What does the ticket include?
faq.a: The guide and entry to the Catacombs of San Gennaro, plus a pass for the Catacombs of San Gaudioso and the Basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità, valid for twelve months and usable on another day. Transport to and from your hotel isn’t included.

faq.q: Can I cancel?
faq.a: Yes, cancellation is free up to 24 hours before your slot, with a full refund. It’s one of the most booked visits in Naples, with over eight thousand reviews, so at weekends it’s worth securing your slot a few days ahead.

114025.intro: Beneath the Basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità lies the city’s second early Christian cemetery: the Catacombs of San Gaudioso, where the African bishop Gaudiosus was buried around 451, and where in the 17th century Neapolitan nobles had themselves buried with their skulls set into the walls for all to see. Forty-five minutes of guided visit, in Italian or English, with a ticket that also covers the Catacombs of San Gennaro within twelve months. One of the strangest and most beautiful things in the neighbourhood.
cosaSiFa: You meet at the catacombs’ ticket office, in the Rione Sanità, a quarter of an hour before your slot. The visit also includes the Basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità above: you see the church first and then go down. The guide tells the story of the place: Gaudiosus’s burial between 451 and 453, his tomb, and the 5th- and 6th-century frescoes and mosaics with early Christian symbols.

Then you move into the 17th-century corridor, from the time when the catacombs were used again to bury the aristocracy: skulls set into the walls, with decorated tombs around them. The frescoes are by Giovanni Balducci, who gave up his fee in exchange for being buried there among the city’s aristocrats. The guide explains the burial rites, the early Christians and 17th-century customs. 45 minutes in all, then you go back up into the basilica.
114025.perChi: For lovers of history and underground Naples who want something more intimate than the Catacombs of San Gennaro, including older kids who won’t be spooked by a skull. Good if you’re short on time, as it’s done in three quarters of an hour. Less suited to the casually punctual: if you arrive after your slot has started, you won’t get in and won’t be refunded.
114025.consiglio: Arrive fifteen minutes early; the rule is strict. It’s cool underground even in summer, so a light sweatshirt helps. The ticket also covers the Catacombs of San Gennaro for a year, in the same neighbourhood: do them the same day or on another visit. Before or after, stop by Palazzo dello Spagnuolo.

faq.q: How long is it and where do we meet?
faq.a: The guided visit lasts 45 minutes and covers the catacombs and the Basilica of Santa Maria della Sanità. Go to the catacombs’ ticket office, in the Rione Sanità, fifteen minutes before your slot. The ticket is only valid for the day and time you chose.

faq.q: Is the ticket also valid for the Catacombs of San Gennaro?
faq.a: Yes: entry to the Catacombs of San Gennaro is included and stays valid for twelve months from your visit, so you can go the same day or on another trip. Both catacombs are in the Rione Sanità, a few minutes apart.

faq.q: What language is the visit in and can I cancel?
faq.a: The guide speaks Italian or English, depending on the slot you choose. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before, with a full refund. If you arrive after your slot has left, you can’t join a later one and you lose the ticket, so don’t be late.

1142689.intro: Three hours in a Neapolitan kitchen with a professional chef, learning two fresh pastas from scratch, fettuccine and ricotta-filled ravioli, plus a hand-whipped tiramisù. You start with eggs and flour, make a sauce with San Marzano DOP tomatoes, and at the end sit down to eat what you’ve made, with a glass of wine or a beer. No experience needed; you leave with the recipes and a diploma.
cosaSiFa: You arrive, put on an apron and hat, and start with a Neapolitan starter while the chef explains the family recipe. Then you knead: fresh eggs and flour, rolling the dough until it’s smooth and elastic, then cutting the fettuccine. Meanwhile the sauce is made with San Marzano tomatoes.

Second pasta, the ravioli: everyone rolls out their sheet, fills it with fresh ricotta and spices and seals their own by hand, one by one. Then it’s on to the tiramisù, with the mascarpone cream worked to the right consistency, the savoiardi (ladyfingers) dipped in coffee, the layers built up slowly and cocoa on top.

At the end everyone sits down with the chef and the other participants: fettuccine Alfredo, ravioli with tomato sauce and the tiramisù, with your chosen drink and unlimited water, finishing with a limoncello. Before you leave you get the recipes via a QR code on your personalised diploma, and a number to call for help when you try it at home.
1142689.perChi: For anyone who has never made pasta at home and wants to go back with two real techniques, and for couples and families: it suits all ages, and under-18s must be accompanied by an adult. Classes run in Italian, English, French and Spanish. Less suited to anyone who just wants to eat without getting behind the counter.
1142689.consiglio: Wear comfortable clothes without bulky sleeves; your hands will be in the flour. Come hungry: you eat everything you make, starter included. Keep the diploma, as the QR code with the recipes really comes in handy when you want to make the ravioli again at home.

faq.q: How long is it and do I need to know how to cook?
faq.a: Three hours, including the cooking and lunch or dinner at the table with the other participants. No experience needed: the chef guides every step, from the dough to the tiramisù. Just bring comfortable clothes and an appetite.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: The class with the chef, apron and hat, a Neapolitan starter, the ingredients for pasta, sauce and tiramisù, a drink of your choice (soft drink, beer or a glass of wine), mineral water, limoncello with dessert, the diploma with the recipe QR code and phone support afterwards.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: It runs in Italian, English, French or Spanish, depending on the date. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before, with a full refund. Suitable for all ages, with under-18s accompanied by an adult.

116146P37.intro: The classic tour of the peninsula in one day, in an air-conditioned vehicle with at most twenty seats and a driver who doubles as your host along the way. You stop at the viewpoint over Positano, spend an hour and a half in Sorrento with a limoncello tasting, and finish with two hours in Pompeii, where you can explore on your own or with a licensed guide if you choose that option. Pickup is at the Stazione Marittima or other points in the city.
cosaSiFa: You leave Naples from the cruise terminal or another agreed point and head by minivan towards the coast. The first stop is the viewpoint over Positano: a short stop to look down on the coloured houses tumbling towards the sea and take a few photos, without going down into the village.

Then Sorrento, with an hour and a half to yourself. Piazza Tasso, Corso Italia with its shops, the cloister of San Francesco and the view over the bay from the terraces. The limoncello tasting included in the price happens here too. Lunch isn’t included: everyone sorts themselves out, with a meeting time set by the driver.

In the afternoon, two hours in Pompeii. The entry ticket isn’t included, and there’s only a guide inside the ruins if you book that option; otherwise you visit at your own pace. The order of the stops may change depending on traffic or the group’s preferences. At the end you head back to Naples.
116146P37.perChi: For anyone who wants to see a lot in a short time in a small vehicle without worrying about timetables, especially cruise passengers and families: the tour is wheelchair accessible with advance notice, pushchairs are allowed and child seats are available. Less suited to anyone wanting an in-depth visit to Pompeii without paying for the guide option.
116146P37.consiglio: Consider the option with a guide at Pompeii: without one, two hours in the ruins with no explanations don’t give you much. Buy your ticket for the ruins in advance so you don’t lose time. In Sorrento, an hour and a half is enough for a walk or a quick lunch, not both at a relaxed pace.

faq.q: How long is it and where does it start?
faq.a: About eight hours. Pickup is available at the Stazione Marittima, the Naples cruise terminal, or at other points in the city; for cruise passengers departure is at 8am, depending on the ship’s schedule. The port of Salerno is only for cruise passengers.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: The air-conditioned minivan with an English-speaking driver-host and commentary on board, pickup, a bottle of water each and the limoncello tasting in Sorrento. Not included: the Pompeii ticket, a guide inside the ruins unless you choose that option, lunch and extra activities.

faq.q: Can I cancel? Is there a minimum number of people?
faq.a: Yes, cancel at least 24 hours before departure for a full refund. The tour needs a minimum number of participants: if it isn’t reached 24 hours before, you can move to another date or reschedule. Available languages are Italian and English.

119305.intro: The Amalfi Coast in a single day, without driving or hunting for parking. You leave Naples in an air-conditioned minibus with a tour leader on board, stop in Sorrento, Positano and Amalfi, and get back in the evening. The group is small, so the stops at the viewpoints are real stops, not drive-bys. Lunch is decided when you book: at a restaurant, arranged in advance, or on your own, with more time to wander.
cosaSiFa: The minibus picks you up at your hotel or at one of the pickup points in the city and reaches Sorrento in about an hour. Here you have seventy free minutes: the old town is small, the giant lemons in the gardens are the thing to see and you can taste limoncello in the shops along the main street. Then you set off along the Amalfi Coast road, which runs along the cliffs high above the sea.

Another hour on the road and you reach Positano: first a short stop for photos from above, then seventy-five minutes on foot among the steps and the beach. From there it’s another hour of bends to Amalfi. Amalfi is the longest stop, an hour and a half, with the cathedral and the little harbour a few steps from where you get off.

In Amalfi you have a choice: if you booked the lunch option, you sit down at an arranged restaurant; if not, you explore on your own. You can also add a boat trip along the coast, optional and paid, which can be booked on the spot if there’s availability. The drive back to Naples takes about an hour and a quarter.
119305.perChi: For anyone with just one day who wants to see all three towns without stress: the minibus does the work, you walk and look. Also good for solo travellers and couples who prefer a small group. Not suitable for people with limited mobility or wheelchair users: these towns are made of steps. No pushchairs or suitcases on board.
119305.consiglio: Comfortable shoes, seriously: Positano is all steps. If you want lunch at a restaurant, choose that option when you book, as it can’t be added later. The boat trip in Amalfi is worth it when the sea is calm. Check your email the day before for the pickup time: the driver waits ten minutes, no more.

faq.q: How long is it and where does it start?
faq.a: About eight and a half hours. Pickup is included, from your hotel or one of the pickup points in the city, including the Stazione Marittima and the Archaeological Museum. The exact time is sent by email: check your inbox the day before departure.

faq.q: What language does the tour leader speak?
faq.a: English, Italian, Spanish or French, depending on the date you choose. The tour can run in two languages at once, so the same explanation may be given twice. The minibus is air-conditioned and water is available on board on request.

faq.q: Is lunch included? Can I cancel?
faq.a: Lunch is only included if you choose the lunch option when booking; otherwise you have free time and eat wherever you like. The boat trip in Amalfi is optional and paid. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before departure.

1242092.intro: The classic Amalfi Coast tour, but with no more than thirteen people on board. You leave from the central station area in an air-conditioned vehicle, with a tour leader who talks you through the road and a driver who knows every bend. The day lasts nine hours and takes in Amalfi, Positano and Sorrento in that order, with photo stops at the best spots. Water is included, lunch isn’t: you eat wherever you like during free time.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Garibaldi and set off: an hour and a half on the road to Amalfi, the longest stop of the day. You have two and a half hours free for the Cathedral of Sant’Andrea, the squares, the shops and a coffee by the harbour. If you like, you can go as far as the Grotta dello Smeraldo (the Emerald Grotto), but time it carefully so you don’t miss the minibus.

Three quarters of an hour of bends and you reach Positano, with an hour to walk down to the beach between the cliffside houses and boutiques. Then another forty-five minutes to Sorrento, for an hour among the lemon groves and the centre, with a taste of limoncello. After that you head back to Naples, an hour and a half to the starting point.
1242092.perChi: For anyone who wants to see all three towns in a day without crowds around them: thirteen people is a minibus, not a coach party. Good if you don’t have a car and don’t want to drive the coast road. The pace is brisk and in some places time flies, so it’s not the choice for anyone who wants to spend hours on the beach.
1242092.consiglio: Get to the meeting point a little early; the group is small and they won’t wait long. Amalfi is the longest stop, so that’s where to have a leisurely lunch. Positano is shorter: take your photo from above and head straight down. Book ahead, as places sell out.

faq.q: Where does it start and how long is it?
faq.a: The meeting point is Piazza Garibaldi, in front of the central station, and that’s where you return at the end of the day. Nine hours in all: three stops in the towns and about four and a half hours on the road, going out, between towns and coming back.

faq.q: What language is the tour in?
faq.a: The tour leader speaks English and Spanish; dates with Italian are shown when you book. The group is limited to thirteen participants, so you can hear well and ask questions easily. Bottled water is included.

faq.q: Is lunch included? Can I cancel?
faq.a: No, lunch isn’t included: you eat during free time, and the longest stop is in Amalfi. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before, and you can book now and pay later, so if you change your mind you lose nothing.

1308037.intro: A 75–90-minute boat trip around the bay, leaving from Santa Lucia at the foot of Castel dell’Ovo. You sail out of the little harbour and see Naples the way people arriving by sea used to: Vesuvius in the background, the castle, then the Posillipo coast with its villas and finally Nisida, the volcanic islet. On board a guide gives live commentary in Italian and English; there’s a covered deck and an open but shaded one, with 360-degree views.
cosaSiFa: Show up at the Santa Lucia quay, in the Borgo Marinari, a quarter of an hour before departure for boarding. The boats carry up to sixty people and have life jackets and safety equipment. Sit wherever you like: under the covered deck or outside in the shade, with a clear view across the whole bay.

As soon as you leave the harbour the skyline opens up: Vesuvius on one side, Castel dell’Ovo seemingly floating on the other. You sail west along the Posillipo coast, with villas perched on the cliffs, as far as Nisida. The guide tells the story of the places, from the Greek colonists to today, with live commentary in Italian and English.

Then you head back to the same spot. 75–90 minutes in all. There are two departures a day, one in the morning and one in the afternoon, from April to November. Boats go out even in uncertain weather; if the sea isn’t safe the trip is cancelled and you’re refunded automatically.
1308037.perChi: It’s the easiest way to see Naples from the sea: no effort, an hour and a quarter sitting down. Good for families with children, couples and anyone short on time. Not recommended for anyone prone to seasickness or for pregnant women. If you want to swim, look for a different trip: this is a sightseeing cruise.
1308037.consiglio: The afternoon departure has the best light on Posillipo. Bring water and a hat: even in the shade, it’s hot in summer. The boarding point is five minutes’ walk from Piazza del Plebiscito, so combine it with the seafront or a stroll around the Borgo Marinari before you board.

faq.q: Where does it leave from and how long is it?
faq.a: It leaves from and returns to the Santa Lucia quay, in the Borgo Marinari, next to Castel dell’Ovo and a few minutes’ walk from Piazza del Plebiscito. It lasts 75 to 90 minutes. You need to be there 15 minutes early for boarding.

faq.q: What’s included and what isn’t?
faq.a: The boat trip, the guide’s live commentary in Italian and English, the covered deck and the shaded outdoor deck, life jackets and safety equipment. Food and drinks, hotel pickup and parking aren’t included.

faq.q: What if the weather’s bad?
faq.a: The cruise runs in most weather conditions. If it’s cancelled because the sea isn’t safe, you get a full automatic refund. Either way, you can cancel for free up to 24 hours before.

1320588.intro: Herculaneum is smaller than Pompeii and better preserved: here the mud of AD 79 sealed in upper floors, wood and frescoes. This tour covers it in half a day, leaving Piazza Garibaldi in an air-conditioned minivan, going in with priority tickets and spending two hours with a licensed guide dedicated to your group. At the end the minivan brings you back to the starting point. The afternoon is yours.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Garibaldi, in front of a hotel next to the station, and get into the minivan. The drive to Herculaneum is short and scenic, with Vesuvius ahead. At the Archaeological Park you meet the guide, who works only with your group, and go in with priority access, skipping the ticket office queue.

The walking visit lasts two hours: everyday Roman life, houses with their upper floors still standing, carbonised materials, mosaics, and the story of the eruption that buried the town. When the tour ends, the minivan takes the group back to Naples, to the same spot you left from. About three hours in all.
1320588.perChi: For anyone who wants to see one of the Vesuvian sites properly and calmly without giving up a whole day, and for those who prefer a guide just for their own group. The tour is in English. Less suited to anyone hoping to combine Pompeii and Herculaneum in one trip: this one visits Herculaneum only.
1320588.consiglio: Bring a camera or a fully charged phone: the interiors of the houses are worth it. Food and drinks aren’t included, so have breakfast first and bring a bottle of water. If you want to carry on to Vesuvius afterwards, ask the guide about connections from Ercolano.

faq.q: How long is it and where does it start?
faq.a: About three hours, two of them on the guided visit inside the park. The meeting point is Piazza Garibaldi, in front of a hotel next to the central station, and the minivan brings you back there at the end.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: Return transport in an air-conditioned minivan, skip-the-line entry tickets for Herculaneum with priority access and the two-hour private guided visit. Food and drinks aren’t included.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: The guide speaks English. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund, and you can book now and pay later. Dates often sell out, so it’s best to book a few days ahead.

141978.intro: Three hours of tastings in a small group, in English, starting and ending in Piazza Dante. Over four or more stops you eat an almond and black pepper tarallo, pizza a portafoglio, a frittatina di pasta, a plate of ragù, and to finish, babà and coffee, with water and a beer included. In between you walk along Via Toledo, San Gregorio Armeno, Piazza San Domenico and Santa Chiara, with the guide explaining where each dish comes from. By the end it’s a full meal, not a snack.
cosaSiFa: You meet in Piazza Dante and head down Via Toledo for the first stop, half an hour: the handmade Neapolitan tarallo, a ring-shaped savoury biscuit with almonds and black pepper, then pizza a portafoglio, folded in four to eat as you walk. You climb back towards the ancient centre, and in San Gregorio Armeno comes the frittatina di pasta, a fried cylinder of pasta, béchamel and peas.

The third stop, near the Cappella Sansevero, is Neapolitan ragù: a proper portion of meat slow-cooked in tomato. Then you carry on towards Santa Chiara for another street food stop. Each stop lasts about half an hour, and between them there are walks of 10 or 15 minutes at a stretch.

The last half hour is for dessert and coffee: a rum-soaked babà and an espresso. The tastings may change with the season and time of day, but the sequence of savoury, hot dish and sweet stays the same. You end back in Piazza Dante. The group is small: for more than twelve people you need to check with the operator first.
141978.perChi: For English speakers who want a lunch or dinner that fills them up for the day and who are happy to walk: couples, friends, families with children, who get a reduced rate. Not suitable for anyone with limited mobility, as there are stretches of continuous walking between stops. If you’re short on time, bear in mind it’s a full three hours.
141978.consiglio: Dress for the weather, because three hours between stops make themselves felt in summer and winter alike. Don’t eat beforehand. Piazza Dante is on metro line 1 and a step away from Port’Alba and the Archaeological Museum: if you book the afternoon slot, do the museum in the morning.

faq.q: What language is the tour in?
faq.a: The guide speaks English. Some slots may run in two languages, Italian and English, but it isn’t guaranteed: if you need Italian, ask before booking. It lasts about three hours, starting and ending in Piazza Dante.

faq.q: What do we eat and what’s included?
faq.a: The guide and tastings at more than four stops are included: tarallo, pizza a portafoglio, frittatina di pasta, ragù, babà and espresso, plus water and an alcoholic drink, usually a beer. The tastings may vary with the season. Extra food and drinks are paid separately.

faq.q: Is it suitable for children?
faq.a: Yes, children are welcome and under-tens get a reduced rate; the youngest go free but still need a ticket. Do factor in three hours and walks of 10 or 15 minutes without a break. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

162012P20.intro: A three-hour class in a venue on Via delle Zite to make fresh egg pasta, ravioli and fettuccine, and a tiramisù from start to finish. You also prepare two sauces, a creamy tomato one and a San Marzano with fresh basil, then sit down to eat what you’ve made with a drink. You go home with the recipes and a personalised diploma.
cosaSiFa: You start with dessert: the tiramisù has to be made first because it needs to rest. Cream, biscuits dipped in coffee, layers and cocoa, with the chef correcting as you go. Meanwhile he explains how handmade pasta is a family affair in southern Italy and what changes with seasonal ingredients.

Then the egg pasta. You knead, roll out and cut the fettuccine, then seal the ravioli using traditional techniques. Meanwhile the two sauces come together: the creamy tomato one and the one with San Marzano tomatoes and fresh basil, to dress what you’ve just made.

Once everything’s cooked, you all sit down and eat: ravioli, fettuccine with the two sauces and, to finish, the tiramisù, with a drink. You leave with a personalised diploma and the written recipes, so you can make it all again at home without guessing the quantities.
162012P20.perChi: For anyone who wants to go home actually knowing how to make something, not just having watched. Works for couples, groups of friends and families; groups can reach 25 people, so don’t expect a private lesson. Three hours standing with your hands in the dough: if you’re short on time or don’t fancy the counter, a shorter tour may suit you better.
162012P20.consiglio: Do it at lunch or dinner time and don’t eat beforehand: pasta with two sauces plus tiramisù is filling. Wear clothes that can get floury. Via delle Zite is a fifteen-minute walk from the central station and the Duomo, handy if you’re arriving by train. Book a few days ahead.

faq.q: What do we make and what’s included?
faq.a: Fresh egg pasta in two shapes, ravioli and fettuccine, two sauces and a tiramisù. You eat everything you make at the end of the class, with a drink. The personalised diploma and recipes are included. It lasts about three hours.

faq.q: What language is the class in?
faq.a: English, Spanish, French and Italian; you choose the language when booking. Groups can be up to 25 people, so the chef moves between the stations explaining as he goes.

faq.q: Can I cancel and where do we meet?
faq.a: Free cancellation up to 24 hours before the start. The meeting point is on Via delle Zite, between the central station and the old town.

162012P38.intro: A three-hour class near Via Duomo where you make the two things everyone wants to learn in Naples: pizza and tiramisù. You start from the flour, knead by hand, stretch the dough and bake it in a traditional oven; then you move on to dessert, layer by layer. You eat what you’ve made, with a starter and a drink included, and go home with the written recipes.
cosaSiFa: You start with the pizza. The chef shows how Neapolitan dough is made from the basic ingredients, then everyone works their own ball of dough: kneading, stretching it by hand, adding the toppings. It’s baked in the traditional oven, and what comes out is your pizza, to eat there and then with the included starter and drink.

The second part is the tiramisù, followed step by step: you make the cream, dip the biscuits, build the layers. At the end everyone has their own dessert. You get the pizza and tiramisù recipes to make them again at home. The class runs in English, Spanish, French or Italian depending on your booking, and lasts about three hours.
162012P38.perChi: Good for couples, groups of friends and families with children who want to get their hands dirty. Groups can reach thirty people, so don’t expect a private lesson: if you want more attention, look for a smaller class. It’s three hours on your feet, so better not to schedule it after a full day of walking.
162012P38.consiglio: Treat it as a meal: you eat a starter, pizza and tiramisù, so skip lunch beforehand. Wear clothes that can get floury. The kitchen is near Via Duomo: beforehand you can see the Duomo and the Chapel of San Gennaro, or wander down San Gregorio Armeno, a few minutes away.

faq.q: What do we make and what do we eat?
faq.a: You make a Neapolitan pizza, from the dough to baking it in a traditional oven, and a tiramisù. You eat what you’ve made, with a starter and a drink included. At the end of the class you get the recipes to make it all again at home.

faq.q: What languages is the class in and how long is it?
faq.a: The class lasts three hours and runs in English, Spanish, French or Italian: you choose the language when booking. Groups can be up to thirty participants, led by a local chef.

faq.q: Where is it and can I cancel?
faq.a: The kitchen is in the Via Duomo area, in the old town of Naples; the exact address comes with your confirmation. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the class starts.

162012P56.intro: Three hours in the kitchen with a local chef on Via delle Zite, making two pastas and a dessert: fettuccine with Alfredo sauce, the butter and Parmigiano one, ricotta-filled ravioli with San Marzano tomato sauce, and tiramisù. You start from the ingredients, fresh ricotta and aged Parmigiano in hand, and finish at the table eating what you’ve made. There’s a diploma at the end.
cosaSiFa: The class opens with an introduction to the ingredients: fresh ricotta, aged Parmigiano, eggs and flour. It helps you understand why pasta turns out well or badly before you even touch it. Then you knead, roll out the sheet and cut the fettuccine, while the chef moves between the stations and straightens out anyone going off course.

The second pasta is ravioli: you make the ricotta filling, seal them one by one and put the San Marzano tomato sauce on. For the fettuccine you make the Alfredo sauce, with butter and Parmigiano. Meanwhile the tiramisù is assembled, as it needs its time in the fridge.

At the end you all eat together at the tables, with the chef sharing local stories and tips to take home. The tiramisù rounds it off. You leave with a certificate of participation. The class is designed for all levels, so nobody gets left behind, not even people who have never kneaded dough.
162012P56.perChi: For families, couples and groups of friends, even large ones: groups go up to thirty people, so it’s the right choice if there are lots of you and you want to stay together. Good for anyone who has never made pasta. If you’d rather have an intimate class with the chef all to yourself, look at the options with ten places.
162012P56.consiglio: Don’t eat beforehand: three hours later you leave with two pastas and a dessert inside you. Via delle Zite is right in the old town: beforehand, a walk along the decumani (the ancient Roman streets) and San Gregorio Armeno, a few minutes away on foot, fits in nicely. Comfortable clothes and short sleeves, as you roll out the pasta with your arms.

faq.q: What language is the class in?
faq.a: The chef speaks Italian, English, Spanish and French; you choose the language when booking. The class lasts three hours and takes place on Via delle Zite, in the old town of Naples. Groups can be up to thirty people.

faq.q: What do we make and what do we eat?
faq.a: Fettuccine with butter and Parmigiano Alfredo sauce, ricotta ravioli with San Marzano tomato sauce, and tiramisù. You eat everything you make at the end of the class, sitting together. The two sauces and the certificate of participation are included.

faq.q: Can I cancel?
faq.a: Yes, cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. The class suits all levels, so no cooking experience is needed: just turn up in comfortable clothes, ready to get your hands dirty.

162012P8.intro: Two hours on foot, downhill, from the Vomero to the centre, by way of the Petraio: the pedestrian stairway that winds down between houses, vegetable gardens and terraces, and that most tourists don’t even know exists. You go up by funicular, included in the ticket, and come down at an easy pace, with the bay, Capri and Vesuvius in front of you at several points. Groups of up to fifteen, with a local guide.
cosaSiFa: You meet in the Vomero, the well-to-do neighbourhood on the hill: elegant buildings, wide streets, a different Naples from the one in the lanes below. The funicular is included in the ticket and covers the uphill part. From here you look down on the city and the guide explains what you’re seeing, from the port to Vesuvius.

Then you join the Petraio and start down: steps, bends, glimpses of the sea between buildings, washing hung out to dry. This is the photogenic part of the walk, and the guide points out the spots to stop. As you descend, the houses and the people change, from grand apartment blocks to working-class streets.

You reach the Quartieri Spagnoli (the Spanish Quarter), with their grid of lanes and stairs where the city feels most itself, and finish in the centre, out on the street, with the rest of the day ahead of you. The stories along the way are about the city and the people who live in it, not just the monuments, and that’s what sets it apart from a classic tour.
162012P8.perChi: For anyone who loves walking and taking photos, and who wants to see Naples from an angle you don’t get from the lanes. The descent is long and all steps: bad knees and pushchairs won’t enjoy it. Good for couples, friends and solo travellers; with fifteen people at most, it’s easy to stay together.
162012P8.consiglio: Shoes with good grip and a bottle of water: there’s a lot of descending. The best light over the bay is in the morning or late afternoon. Before you start, it’s worth going up to Castel Sant’Elmo or the Certosa di San Martino, both in the Vomero with the same view; afterwards, the Quartieri Spagnoli and Via Toledo are right there.

faq.q: How much walking is there and how long is it?
faq.a: The tour lasts about two hours, almost all on foot and downhill, from the Vomero to the centre via the Petraio, a pedestrian stairway. You go up by funicular, included in the ticket. You need comfortable shoes and legs in decent shape.

faq.q: What languages is it available in?
faq.a: Italian, English, Spanish and French; you choose the language when booking. Groups are up to fifteen people, with a local guide who stays with you the whole way and shares stories and curiosities about the neighbourhoods you pass through.

faq.q: What’s included and how do I cancel?
faq.a: The local guide and the funicular are included. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the start, with a full refund. Available start times are shown when you book, depending on the date you choose.

162012P9.intro: Two hours on foot between the old town and the Pignasecca market, with six stops to eat: you open with a spritz and a board of cured meats and mozzarella, continue with tarallo, pizza a portafoglio and a cuoppo of fried fish, then a meatball in ragù, and finish with sfogliatella or gelato and a limoncello or a coffee. The guide tells stories and legends of the neighbourhood between bites.
cosaSiFa: Meet in Piazza Carità, a step from the Pignasecca. You start with a spritz and a board of cured meats and mozzarella to break the ice, while the guide explains how the market works and where the things you’re about to eat come from, in places where Neapolitans actually go.

Then you walk and eat: a tarallo, a folded pizza a portafoglio to hold in your hand, and the cuoppo, a paper cone of fried fish. The fifth stop is a meatball slow-cooked in ragù. You’re among the market stalls and eateries, with the guide’s stories and tips between one bite and the next.

You finish with dessert: sfogliatella (the shell-shaped pastry) or artisan gelato, your choice, with a limoncello or an espresso. There’s a vegetarian option, to be requested when booking. About two hours in all, six tastings and dessert.
162012P9.perChi: For anyone who wants to eat the way people eat here, standing up and without sitting down in a restaurant. Good for couples and groups of friends, and for anyone short on time: two hours and you’ve had a full meal. Works with children if they eat everything. If you have allergies or intolerances, say so in advance; there’s a vegetarian version.
162012P9.consiglio: Come on an empty stomach, really: six stops with pizza, fried food and a meatball make a big lunch. Comfortable shoes and no bulky bags, as it’s a tight squeeze between the market stalls. Piazza Carità is on Via Toledo: afterwards, the Galleria Umberto and Piazza del Plebiscito are ten minutes downhill.

faq.q: What do we eat on the tour?
faq.a: A spritz with a board of cured meats and mozzarella, a tarallo, a pizza a portafoglio, a cuoppo of fried fish, a meatball in ragù and a dessert, either sfogliatella or gelato, with limoncello or coffee. A vegetarian option is available.

faq.q: What language is it in and how long is it?
faq.a: English, Spanish, French and Italian. It lasts about two hours, in groups of up to fifteen people.

faq.q: Where does it start and can I cancel?
faq.a: Meet in Piazza Carità, at the start of the Pignasecca. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

165716.intro: The volcano and the city it buried, on the same day and in the right order: first you climb to the crater, then you head down to Pompeii with a guide. You leave from Piazza Garibaldi in an air-conditioned coach, with tickets for Pompeii and Vesuvius National Park already included. Between the two stops you eat a pizza with a soft drink, covered by the tour. It’s one of the most booked trips from Naples, with thousands of reviews.
cosaSiFa: Meet in front of the central station, in Piazza Garibaldi, and set off for Vesuvius. The coach climbs to about 1,000 metres, then you spend an hour and a half on foot, between the climb to the crater, the local guide’s explanations of the volcano and a stop to look down over the bay. On the way back there’s a lunch break, forty-five minutes in a restaurant with pizza and a soft drink.

In the afternoon you enter Pompeii for a two-hour guided visit. You pass through the Forum, the Lupanar (the ancient brothel), a thermopolium (a Roman street-food counter) and the Stabian Baths, with the guide describing life in the city before the eruption of AD 79: bakeries, theatres, frescoes and mosaics. After the visit the coach takes everyone back to Piazza Garibaldi.
165716.perChi: For anyone with one day who wants to tick off Vesuvius and Pompeii without changing transport three times. Good for families; people who have done it with their kids speak well of it. You need a basic level of fitness: the climb to the crater is a sloping path. The guide speaks English or Spanish, not Italian.
165716.consiglio: Bring valid ID, as it’s requested on the day. Closed shoes and a hat: on Vesuvius the sun beats down and the gravel is slippery. In rain or strong wind the crater may be closed, in which case you only do Pompeii. The departure time is indicative: wait for the agency’s confirmation with the exact time and place.

faq.q: How long is it and where does it start?
faq.a: From three and a half to eight hours, depending on the option: the full day with Vesuvius, lunch and Pompeii is the long one. You leave from and return to Piazza Garibaldi, in front of the central station. The exact time is confirmed by the agency after booking.

faq.q: What does the price include?
faq.a: A return air-conditioned coach, a tour guide, commentary on board, lunch with pizza and a soft drink, entry to Pompeii and a ticket for Vesuvius National Park. Remember valid ID, as it’s requested on the day of the tour.

faq.q: What language is the guide? Can I cancel?
faq.a: The guide speaks English or Spanish; Italian isn’t among the listed languages. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before departure, and you can book now and pay later. The group is small.

165824P1.intro: A three-hour walk between the Galleria Umberto I and the Quartieri Spagnoli, with six tastings and three drinks along the way. The theme is the food of Naples when it was the capital of a kingdom: dishes once served at court that are still eaten in the lanes today. You taste pasta, mop up the sauce with bread, move on to pizza margherita and finish with a sfogliatella. Small group, twelve people at most, with an English-speaking guide.
cosaSiFa: You start from the Galleria Umberto I, a few steps from Via Toledo. The first stops set the scene: what the kings and queens of Naples ate and how those dishes made their way onto everyone’s table. You walk and stop at places in the centre, each for a different tasting, while the guide tells the story.

Then you head up into the Quartieri Spagnoli, where the guide shares the neighbourhood’s legends and traditions between stops. This is where the heartier part comes: a plate of Neapolitan-style pasta, with bread for the scarpetta, mopping up every last drop of sauce, and a pizza margherita made the way it is here.

The finale is sweet, with a sfogliatella in a local café. Six tastings and three drinks in all, spread over the three hours, so it’s best to arrive hungry and skip the previous meal. At the end you’re still in the centre, a few minutes from Via Toledo and Piazza del Plebiscito.
165824P1.perChi: Made for anyone who wants to eat Neapolitan food without hunting for places on their own and prefers a small group, twelve people at most. The guide only speaks English: if you don’t follow it well, you’ll miss out on the stories. You walk for three hours, including uphill in the Quartieri; a pushchair can be awkward. Not for anyone in a hurry.
165824P1.consiglio: Book it for lunch or dinner time and arrive on an empty stomach: six tastings are a full meal. Comfortable shoes, because the Quartieri Spagnoli are uphill. Before or after, take a look around the Galleria Umberto I and Piazza del Plebiscito, right next door.

faq.q: How long is it and how many tastings are there?
faq.a: The tour lasts three hours and includes six tastings and three drinks, from pasta to pizza margherita to sfogliatella. You walk between the centre and the Quartieri Spagnoli, stopping at different places. Groups are limited to twelve people.

faq.q: What language is it in?
faq.a: The guide speaks English. No other languages are offered, so only book it if you can comfortably follow three hours of explanations in English. The food part, of course, needs no translation.

faq.q: Where’s the meeting point and how do I cancel?
faq.a: You meet at the Galleria Umberto I, in the centre of Naples, near Via Toledo and Piazza del Plebiscito; the exact details come with your confirmation. You can cancel for free up to 24 hours before the start.

165824P2.intro: Three and a half hours in the old town eating pizza in all its forms: at least six kinds, from the classic to the fried, in local pizzerias chosen by an English-speaking guide. Between tastings you walk the UNESCO stretch between Port’Alba and the Decumani, step into a church and drink a spritz in the roof garden of a 15th-century palazzo. Small group, twelve people at most.
cosaSiFa: You start from Port’Alba, the 1625 gate linking Piazza Dante to the street of booksellers. The first stop is at a place in the old town that has been going for over fifty years, for pizza with scarola (escarole), olives and walnuts: Neapolitan peasant cooking, twenty minutes. Then Piazza del Gesù, with the story of the façade of the Gesù Nuovo and its wartime miracle.

Second stop, the montanara: fried dough, tomato and cheese, the street food that legend says King Ferdinand of Bourbon loved. Another twenty minutes of tasting and off you go again. Forty minutes later you’re inside a palazzo from 1412, once the embassy of the Republic of Venice, with a spritz in the roof garden among art and history.

You carry on towards Piazzetta Nilo and the Decumani with more pizzas, ending with a small dessert. Stops and tastings may change depending on the day and the season, but the total is always at least six different pizzas, from the classics to more modern ones like the fried version. You finish with a full stomach and no need for dinner.
165824P2.perChi: For anyone who wants to understand pizza in Naples beyond the margherita, and who’d rather be guided by a local than pick places at random. The guide only speaks English. Vegetarian and gluten-free diets can be accommodated if you mention them when booking; not suitable for anyone with serious food allergies. Under-fours join for free, without food.
165824P2.consiglio: Don’t have lunch beforehand: six pizzas is a lot, even by the slice. Arrive at the meeting point a quarter of an hour early; the confirmation email on your phone is all you need. The tour needs at least two participants to go ahead, so it’s a safer bet as a couple or with friends.

faq.q: How long is it and where does it start?
faq.a: About three and a half hours. The meeting point is Port’Alba, the gate between Piazza Dante and the old town, in front of a bookshop: you’ll recognise the guide by the purple bag. Best to arrive fifteen minutes early so you can leave on time.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: At least six different pizzas in pizzerias in the centre, a classic spritz, a small dessert and the local English-speaking guide with tips about the city. Extra drinks, tips and transport to and from your hotel aren’t included.

faq.q: Is it suitable for children and can I cancel?
faq.a: Children under four join for free but without food; from four upwards they need a ticket with tastings included. Cancel at least 24 hours before the scheduled start for a full refund.

18971P114.intro: A small-group pasta and tiramisù class, ten people at most, on Via Medina, a short walk from Piazza Municipio. You make two kinds of pasta by hand and a tiramisù with a chef who explains in Italian and English, and at the end you sit down to eat the results with a starter and a glass of wine. It lasts two to two and a half hours depending on the group size. Diploma, recipe book and luggage storage included.
cosaSiFa: You start with the tiramisù, which needs to rest while you work on everything else. The chef explains each step and has everyone do it, in Italian and English depending on who’s at the counter, from the mascarpone cream to the layers with biscuits and cocoa.

Then the fresh pasta: flour, eggs and hands. You knead, roll out and shape two different kinds of pasta, with the chef correcting thickness and cut. With ten people at most, there’s time for every question and to redo a step if it didn’t come out right.

At the end you sit round the table and eat what you’ve made, with the starter and a glass of wine; the tiramisù closes the meal. You leave with the diploma and the recipe book, and if you left your suitcases in storage, you pick them up on the way out.
18971P114.perChi: For anyone who has just checked out of their hotel or has a train to catch and wants to make good use of two hours: the luggage storage solves the problem. Small group, so it also works if you’re starting from zero in the kitchen. Couples, friends, families with older kids who want to get their hands dirty.
18971P114.consiglio: Book a time that coincides with lunch or dinner: after pasta and tiramisù you won’t eat anything else. Via Medina is five minutes from the Maschio Angioino and the Municipio metro stop, and handy from the port too. If you have luggage, use the storage and add a walk to Piazza del Plebiscito afterwards.

faq.q: How long is the class?
faq.a: Between two and two and a half hours, depending on the size of the group, which is ten people at most. The pace adapts to whoever is there.

faq.q: What’s included?
faq.a: The class with the chef, the ingredients for two kinds of pasta and for the tiramisù, a starter and a glass of wine at the table, the recipe book, the diploma and luggage storage.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: English, Spanish, French and Italian; the chef runs the class in Italian and English. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before. The meeting point is on Via Medina.

18971P130.intro: A two-and-a-half-hour class near Via Medina, designed for anyone who wants to make pizza at home for real: not in a wood-fired oven, but in the ruoto, the round baking tin Neapolitan families use, baked in a home oven. You knead, stretch and bake, then make tiramisù with mascarpone. Fifteen people at most, apron and digital recipe book included, and you can leave your suitcase.
cosaSiFa: You start with the dough: the chef explains the proportions and the technique, then everyone works their own. You stretch it into the ruoto and bake it in a home oven, so what you learn can be repeated without special equipment. Meanwhile you have the starter and something to drink; there’s an option with unlimited wine.

The second part is the tiramisù: mascarpone cream, biscuits and coffee, built up in layers. At the end everyone eats their own pizza and dessert, taking their time. The digital recipe book lets you make it all again at home. Allergies and intolerances must be mentioned when booking.
18971P130.perChi: Good for anyone who already cooks a bit and wants to take home a useful technique, and for families and couples looking for an afternoon without much walking. The group is small, fifteen at most. Handy on your last day too, before the train: you can leave your luggage. Not for anyone after wood-fired pizza.
18971P130.consiglio: Via Medina is a stone’s throw from the Maschio Angioino and Piazza Municipio: pair the class with a visit to the castle or the port. Arrive hungry, because between starter, pizza and tiramisù it’s a full meal. If you have an afternoon train, make use of the luggage storage.

faq.q: What’s included in the class?
faq.a: Apron, ingredients, starter and a drink, the digital recipe book and luggage storage. There’s an option with unlimited wine. You eat the pizza and tiramisù you make during the class, so it counts as a meal.

faq.q: How long is it and how many people take part?
faq.a: The class lasts about two and a half hours, in a group of up to fifteen people led by a local chef. It runs in Italian, English, Spanish or French, chosen when booking.

faq.q: Can I flag allergies and cancel?
faq.a: Yes: allergies and intolerances must be flagged when booking, as the operator requests. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before the class starts.

18971P22.intro: The walking tour that brings the two Naples together: the grand one around Piazza del Plebiscito and the one of the lanes in the ancient centre. You start from the Neptune Fountain, pass the Maschio Angioino, the San Carlo and the Galleria, walk up Via Toledo and into the Decumani as far as San Gregorio Armeno. Then you go down beneath San Lorenzo Maggiore, where the Roman streets survive, ticket included. If you like, you finish with lunch.
cosaSiFa: Meet in Piazza Municipio, at the Neptune Fountain, with the time confirmed via the booking panel. The guide introduces the history of the city and you walk towards Castel Nuovo, the Teatro di San Carlo, the Galleria Umberto I, Piazza Trieste e Trento and Piazza del Plebiscito, the grand stretch of royal Naples.

From there you take Via Toledo into the old town: Via San Gregorio Armeno with its nativity-scene workshops, and Via dei Tribunali. Beneath the Basilica of San Lorenzo Maggiore, the guided visit to the Roman remains lasts about three quarters of an hour, entry included. The three-hour tour ends between Piazza Bellini and Piazza del Gesù Nuovo.

If you choose the longer option, you stop for an hour for lunch: caprese, spaghetti with tomato sauce or carbonara, tiramisù, a glass of house wine and a bottle of water. In that case the tour ends after the meal. Groups can reach forty people, with headsets when needed to hear the guide clearly.
18971P22.perChi: For first-timers in Naples who want a clear picture of the city in one morning, from palaces to lanes, with a slice of the underground thrown in. There’s a fair amount of walking, so you need reasonable fitness. Less suited to anyone looking for a small group: it’s a large tour, with headsets.
18971P22.consiglio: Comfortable shoes and clothes for the weather, because the tour runs even in the rain. If you book lunch, flag allergies and intolerances straight away. Cruise passengers must give their ship and times when booking. The minimum is two participants from April to October, four in winter.

faq.q: How long is it and where do we meet?
faq.a: Three hours for the walk alone, four with lunch. The meeting point is Piazza Municipio, at the Neptune Fountain; the meeting time must be confirmed via the booking panel and differs from the listed start time.

faq.q: What’s included in the price?
faq.a: The guided walking tour with a licensed guide, the ticket for the underground Roman ruins of San Lorenzo Maggiore and headsets when the group needs them. The meal is only included if you choose the lunch option. Tips and hotel transport are excluded.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: The tour is available in Italian, English and Spanish. Cancel at least 24 hours before the scheduled start for a full refund. If the minimum number of participants isn’t reached, you’ll be offered an alternative or a refund.

18971P4.intro: A day on the Amalfi Coast that focuses on two towns instead of three: Amalfi, the old maritime republic, and Ravello, the village high up on the terraces. You travel in an air-conditioned vehicle with a tour leader on board who talks you through the coast, with photo stops and a limoncello tasting. Time in the towns is yours, with no compulsory guided visits, and if you like you can add a boat trip from Amalfi.
cosaSiFa: The driver picks you up at your hotel, where the service is available, or at the meeting point near the station, and you set off towards the Sorrento peninsula. The first stop is short, a quarter of an hour at a viewpoint for photos, before joining the coast road. Meanwhile the tour leader shares local stories and legends.

In Amalfi you have an hour and a half free: the Cathedral of Sant’Andrea, the squares, the harbour. The optional half-hour shared boat trip leaves from here, to see villas and cliffs from the sea. Then you climb to Ravello for an hour and a quarter: gardens, terraces and a calmer atmosphere. The drive back to Naples rounds off the day.
18971P4.perChi: For anyone who has already seen Positano or prefers the quieter side of the coast: Ravello is less crowded and has views no other town can match. Groups can reach thirty people, so it’s not an intimate tour. Not recommended for anyone with back problems, pregnant women or people with heart conditions: the road is all bends.
18971P4.consiglio: Choose the boat option when you book if you want to see Amalfi from the sea: half an hour is enough. In Ravello bring water and a hat, as you walk uphill and there’s little shade. Lunch isn’t included: you have more time in Amalfi, so that’s the place to eat. Confirm your pickup time beforehand, as it differs from the departure time.

faq.q: How long is it and where does it start?
faq.a: Eight hours in all. Pickup is door to door where possible, and the exact time is confirmed the day before. For last-minute bookings the only pickup point is near the station, in Piazza Garibaldi. The driver waits ten minutes for latecomers, then leaves.

faq.q: What language is it in?
faq.a: The tour leader speaks English, Italian, Spanish, French or Portuguese, depending on the date. The tour may run in two languages on the same day. It’s a shared group of up to thirty participants; in low season departure is confirmed with at least four people, in high season with two.

faq.q: What’s included and how do I cancel?
faq.a: Return transport with air conditioning, a tour leader on board, photo stops, a limoncello tasting and water on request. The boat trip is only included if you choose that option. Lunch and tips are excluded. Free cancellation up to 24 hours before.

18971P46.intro: Two and a half hours on a sailing boat, in a group of up to twelve, leaving from Molo Marinelli and following the Naples coastline to Posillipo. You pass Castel dell’Ovo and the Bourbon-era villas overlooking the sea, with Vesuvius, Capri and the Sorrento peninsula in the background, and stop for a swim when the weather allows. On board there’s a welcome drink and something to nibble as the sun goes down.
cosaSiFa: You board at Molo Marinelli in the late afternoon, cast off and head out with the city sliding past alongside. The first stretch runs past Castel dell’Ovo, then you continue towards Posillipo, where the hill drops sheer into the water and the Bourbon villas are easier to see from the sea than from the road, because from the road you can hardly see them at all.

At Posillipo, if the sea is calm and the season allows, the boat stops for a swim. The water here is cleaner than you’d expect from a city this size, and diving in with a view of Vesuvius is usually the part that stays with you. If you’d rather not get wet, stay on board with a glass in hand.

On the way back comes the sunset: the welcome drink, a spritz, with some crunchy nibbles, and the bay changing colour with Capri and the Sorrento coast ahead. You get back to the jetty as darkness is almost falling, in time for dinner, with the salt still on your skin.
18971P46.perChi: For couples, groups of friends and anyone who wants to see Naples from the sea without the chaos of the ferries: twelve people at most, slow pace. Also fine if you’ve never set foot on a sailing boat. If you get seasick, think it over, and if you’re travelling with young children, bear in mind it’s two and a half hours on board without going ashore.
18971P46.consiglio: Bring a swimsuit and towel, ideally with the swimsuit already on, so no time is lost at Posillipo. You’ll also want a sweatshirt: out on the water at sunset the air changes, even in summer. The exact boarding point and time, which follows the sunset, come with your confirmation: be there a few minutes early. With only twelve places, book ahead.

faq.q: Where does the boat leave from and how long is it?
faq.a: It leaves from Molo Marinelli, in central Naples, and you’re at sea for about two and a half hours, with the timing following the sunset. Groups are up to twelve people. Italian, English, Spanish and French are spoken on board.

faq.q: Can we swim?
faq.a: Yes, there’s a swim stop in the waters off Posillipo, if sea conditions allow. Bring a swimsuit and towel. If you’d rather not get wet, stay on board: the boat is still and the view of Vesuvius is the same.

faq.q: What’s included and how do I cancel?
faq.a: Small-group sailing, a welcome drink (a spritz) and some crunchy nibbles are included. Cancellation is free up to 24 hours before departure, with a full refund.

18971P68.intro: A full day combining the three things everyone passing through Naples always asks for: the Amalfi Coast seen from above, Sorrento and Pompeii. You travel in an air-conditioned coach with commentary on board, stop to photograph the bay, taste limoncello where it’s made, get two free hours in Sorrento and finish with a guided visit to the ruins, ticket included. Designed for anyone short on time, cruise passengers included.
cosaSiFa: The coach collects participants at various points in Naples, including Molo Beverello, with the pickup time confirmed the day before based on where you’re staying. Along the Sorrento peninsula there are photo stops over the bay, then a twenty-minute stop at a limoncello workshop to taste the liqueur and other lemon products.

You continue to the panoramic terrace over Positano, a quarter of an hour to look down on the vertical village and take photos. Then Sorrento, with two free hours: the shopping street, the cloister of San Francesco, a gelato or lunch, which is only included if chosen when booking.

The afternoon is for Pompeii. The guide takes the group into the ruins for an hour and a half to two hours: the Forum, one of the baths, some shops and a domus (a Roman house). The ticket is included and there’s no need to queue at the ticket office. Towards evening the coach takes everyone back to Naples, to the same points where they were picked up in the morning.
18971P68.perChi: For anyone with just one day who wants to take in the coast, Sorrento and Pompeii without organising trains and ferries, cruise passengers included. Not suitable for anyone with back or cardiovascular problems, pregnant women or anyone who has trouble walking: Pompeii requires good fitness. Babies travel on a lap.
18971P68.consiglio: In Sorrento the two hours fly by: decide beforehand whether you’d rather have lunch or explore. Bring comfortable shoes and water for the ruins, which are sun-baked in the afternoon. The tour runs rain or shine, and in low season it needs at least six participants to be confirmed.

faq.q: Where does it start and at what time?
faq.a: Pickup is at various points in Naples, including Molo Beverello, and straight from the ship for cruise passengers. The exact time differs from the tour’s start time: it’s confirmed via the booking panel based on where you’re staying.

faq.q: What’s included and what isn’t?
faq.a: Return transport from Naples, panoramic stops, commentary on board, a live guide at Pompeii and the entry ticket to the ruins. Lunch is only included if selected when booking. Tips and optional activities are at your own expense.

faq.q: What language is it in and can I cancel?
faq.a: The tour is available in Italian, English and Spanish and may run bilingually. Cancel at least 24 hours before the scheduled start for a full refund. The day lasts about eight hours, travel included.
